candidate.answerReason: The midpoint conditions imply AF=2BF, so BA=3BF=15.

methods.label: Apply the midsegment theorem twice
methods.explanation:
Because \(BD\) is a median, \(D\) is the midpoint of \(AC\). Also, \(BE=ED\) makes \(E\) the midpoint of \(BD\). These two midpoint conditions suggest using triangle midsegments twice.

First, \(F\) is strictly between \(A\) and \(B\): \(F=B\) would contradict \(BF=5\), while \(F=A\) would force \(E=D\), contradicting \(BE=ED\).

Let \(G\) be the midpoint of \(AF\). In triangle \(ACF\), the segment joining midpoints \(D\) and \(G\) is parallel to \(CF\). Now let \(H\) be the midpoint of \(BG\). In triangle \(BDG\), the segment \(EH\) is parallel to \(DG\).

Since \(C,E,F\) are collinear, \(EF\) is also parallel to \(DG\). There is only one parallel to \(DG\) through \(E\), so \(EH\) and \(EF\) are the same line. Their intersection with \(BG\) gives \(H=F\). Consequently, \(BF=FG\). Also, \(AG=GF\) because \(G\) is the midpoint of \(AF\).

The points occur along \(AB\) in the order \(A,G,F,B\), so
\[
BA=AG+GF+FB=3BF=3\cdot5=\boxed{15}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
methods.levelReason: This construction uses the elementary midsegment theorem, uniqueness of a parallel line, and addition of segment lengths.

methods.label: Use equal areas from the midpoint conditions
methods.explanation:
Write \([PQR]\) for the area of triangle \(PQR\). A median divides a triangle into equal areas: because \(AD=DC\), triangles \(ABD\) and \(CBD\) have equal bases on \(AC\) and the same altitude from \(B\).

Because \(BE=ED\), triangles \(ABE\) and \(ADE\) each have half the area of \(ABD\). Likewise, \(BCE\) and \(CDE\) each have half the area of \(CBD\). Thus these four small triangles all have the same positive area, say \(k\). It follows that
\[
[ACE]=[ADE]+[CDE]=2k,
\qquad [BCE]=k.
\]
The point \(E\) lies inside triangle \(ABC\), so along \(CF\) the order is \(C,E,F\). Replacing base \(CE\) by \(CF\) multiplies both areas \([ACE]\) and \([BCE]\) by the same positive factor \(CF/CE\). Therefore
\[
\frac{[ACF]}{[BCF]}=\frac{[ACE]}{[BCE]}=2.
\]
But triangles \(ACF\) and \(BCF\) have the same altitude from \(C\) to \(AB\), so this area ratio is also \(AF/BF\). Hence \(AF=2BF\), and
\[
BA=AF+BF=3BF=3\cdot5=\boxed{15}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
methods.levelReason: Equal-base and common-altitude area comparisons provide an elementary alternative that needs no similarity, coordinates, or vectors.
